items.title: Slide Hampton interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003
items.q: all the musicians that you hear playing the small groups that we aspired to, like Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie and Benny Goodman, Stan Getz, they all were raised in the big band period.

ctx.x: Well you have done both small group and big band music. Is there a place that you’re most comfortable in?

You know you’re thinking — of course I’ve been asked that question many times and most musicians are. But see the thing is that we actually were raised in the big band period. And all the musicians that you hear playing the small groups that we aspired to, like Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie and Benny Goodman, Stan Getz, they all were raised in the big band period. And that was what prepared them so well to be so well presented in small groups, that big band experience. So actually we find both of them as…
It might seem obvious to musicians what that positive experience of being in a big band is, but maybe for non-musicians who might see this tape, can you relate what kind of things you gain from that?

items.title: Slide Hampton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So I know Benny’s a very difficult guy and all that, but he sure in hell stood up for something that a lot of people don’t.

ctx.x: That’s 30 years before Woody Herman had this band.

Yeah. So I know Benny’s a very difficult guy and all that, but he sure in hell stood up for something that a lot of people don’t. Maybe that’s because he was an arrogant guy, but nevertheless, he stood up for it.
You’re saying Woody Herman’s cut from the same cloth?
